gist: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick argue that a vertical hyperscaler capex cycle (a rolling three-year forward consensus now above $3 trillion versus $500 billion in December 2022) is the single force overriding every macro shock, and that emerging markets at 9.9x forward earnings have quietly become a cheaper pure-play on the same AI trade than the S&P 500 at 20x. They pair that with behavioral data on retail speculation — one in four men aged 18-29 claiming daily stock trading with two-thirds feeling like failures, $3.9 trillion of cumulative US gambling losses since 1929, and SpaceX SPV investors who expected $300,000 and got $45,000.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler capex as the market's load-bearing wall

insights.claim: Bloomberg consensus for the rolling three-year forward sum of capex at Amazon, Google, Meta, Oracle and Microsoft has surpassed $3 trillion, up from roughly $500 billion when the series started in December 2022.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: The single number to track for the AI trade: the second derivative of this curve flattening is the sell signal for the whole earnings complex.
insights.quote: Bloomer consensus on a rolling basis now surpassed $3 trillion.

insights.claim: The hosts attribute the equity market's indifference to a decade of shocks — pandemic, 9% inflation, Fed hikes, Silicon Valley Bank, tariffs and Liberation Day, two wars, the yen carry trade unwind, Evergrande, the predicted commercial real estate and private credit crashes — primarily to the AI trade rather than to any macro improvement.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: If AI is the sole load-bearing narrative, hedging macro headlines is wasted money and the only hedge that matters is against AI capex disappointment.
insights.quote: Ben, you're right. AI is the only thing that matters.

insights.claim: Because hyperscalers are funding the AI buildout from real earnings rather than being unprofitable startups, the market's downside is tied to those same companies slowing their spending rather than to a financing accident.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Watch capex guidance, not credit spreads, for the turn — the earnings that support the index are the same earnings being spent.
insights.quote: the hyperscalers are powering a lot of the earnings growth that we're seeing because they're the ones doing the spending. And if and when they slow down, the market's going to come come down with it.

insights.claim: The bull case for continued AI capex rests on trusting that seven to ten of the largest companies ever created are spending rationally toward an eventual return on capital, and the hosts explicitly take that side.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Frames the short thesis honestly: bearish AI capex requires believing the best-capitalized managements in history are simultaneously wrong.
insights.quote: And if you're betting against that, you're betting against like seven to 10 of the biggest and best companies that have ever been created that they have no idea what they're doing.

insights.claim: A Columbia Business School professor writing in Bloomberg estimates AI infrastructure investment at roughly 2.8% of US GDP, larger than the railroad boom, and argues the US would be in recession without it.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Sizes AI capex as a macro-scale stimulus, meaning any capex digestion phase shows up in GDP prints, not just in tech earnings.
insights.quote: He estimates AI infrastructure investment at roughly 2.8% of GDP, larger than the railroad boom, and is projected to keep rising.

insights.claim: The hosts assign roughly 80% odds that AI is the proximate cause of the next US recession.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Implies recession-hedging should be expressed through AI-capex-sensitive assets (semis, power, data center REITs) rather than classic cyclicals.
insights.quote: And if you listed what will the reason be for the next recession, I would put AI as like 80% favorites.

themes.theme: All-time highs, earnings, and a narrow breadth trap

insights.claim: The S&P 500 has made roughly 1,379 all-time highs since 1950, about 7% of all trading days, with 26 already this year versus an average of about 21 per year since 1990.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: All-time highs cluster in regimes — the 2000-2012 stretch had years with zero — so treating each new high as a distribution signal has been historically costly.

insights.claim: Bank of America data cited on the show puts S&P 500 Q2 EPS on pace for 30% year-over-year growth excluding investment markups on private stakes, versus roughly 50% including them.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A 20-point wedge between headline and core earnings growth comes from marking private AI stakes — investors should back out the non-repeatable portion when valuing mega-caps.

insights.claim: Part of recent mega-cap earnings growth is non-repeatable mark-ups on private holdings of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX carried by Amazon and Alphabet.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Private AI marks are now a live earnings-quality issue; a down round anywhere in that cluster reverses into reported EPS.

insights.claim: Year to date the Russell 2000 is up about 22%, the equal-weight S&P 500 about 16% and the cap-weighted S&P about 14%, yet only 45% of companies are beating the index.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Broadening at the index level without broadening at the stock level means the apparent stock-picker's market is a trap for active managers.

insights.claim: Outperformance this year is concentrated in sectors most portfolios barely own: 86% of energy stocks, 64% of materials, and about 60% each of technology and industrials are beating the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Explains why active performance can lag in a broadening tape — the breadth is in low-weight sectors most managers are structurally underweight.

themes.theme: Emerging markets as the cheap AI proxy

insights.claim: The MSCI Emerging Markets Index trades at 9.9 times next year's estimated earnings versus 20 times for the S&P 500 — a record discount — even though EM has outperformed for the past two years and is up around 20% this year against the S&P's 14%.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A record valuation gap alongside positive relative momentum is an unusual setup for adding EM exposure rather than fading it.

insights.claim: Taiwan and South Korea now make up 45-46% of the emerging markets index, China another 20% and India 12%, with technology at 41% of the index, making EM more concentrated than the US market and effectively an AI play.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Investors buying EM for diversification are actually doubling their AI/semiconductor beta — check overlap before sizing.

insights.claim: The hosts frame the choice as owning Samsung, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semi at roughly 10x forward earnings versus the US hyperscalers and Nasdaq at 20x, and say that comparison would have sounded absurd five years ago.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A concrete relative-value expression of the AI trade: same theme, half the multiple, different position in the value chain.
insights.quote: it's basically saying, would you rather own Samsung and SKHEX or the hyperscalers

insights.claim: Consensus 2026 earnings growth expectations for Korea are roughly 250% versus about 25% for the all-country world index, which the hosts say is both unsustainable and the reason Korean equities screen so cheap.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: The EM discount is partly an artifact of unbelievable forward estimates — a reason to stress-test the 10x multiple before treating it as cheap.

insights.claim: South Korean retail participation in the equity market has more than doubled from under 10% through the 2010s to 28%, while South Korean households still hold 77% of assets in real estate, 9% in cash and only 3.6% in equities and bonds.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A structural domestic bid for Korean and Taiwanese equities that is barely started — the local flow story, not just the AI story, supports EM multiples.
insights.quote: I don't think people are ready for the the wave of money coming into stocks from younger people in other countries.

insights.claim: The hosts argue Asia is at its own dot-com moment for equity ownership, comparable to the US move from roughly 30% to 60% household stock ownership during the dot-com bubble.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: If the analogy holds, local retail flows can sustain elevated Asian equity valuations for years before the reflexive unwind.

themes.theme: Crash mechanics: air pockets over 1987 repeats

insights.claim: Michael Burry has published a call that markets are near a major top with a possible 1987-type fall, which the hosts treat as unforecastable while noting his January 2023 'sell' call preceded a doubling of the market.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A reminder that the cost of permabearish positioning is measured in doublings, not drawdowns.

insights.claim: The hosts partially agree with Burry that modern market structure and information speed make a single-day 7-12% air pocket a materially higher probability event than in the past, even though they reject a 1987-style rout.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Argues for owning convexity/tail hedges rather than reducing equity exposure — the risk is speed of repricing, not a slow bear market.
insights.quote: a an air pocket situation is way a much higher probability event than it was in the past

insights.claim: The hosts note that speed cuts both ways, citing Microsoft going from a 35% drawdown at the beginning of July to within 5-6% of all-time highs.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Round-trip speed in mega-caps punishes both panic selling and slow rebalancing; drawdown-based de-risking rules are increasingly whipsaw-prone.
insights.quote: at the beginning of July, Microsoft was in a 35% draw down. Now it's five or 6% from all-time highs.

insights.claim: The hosts float the near-collapse of the Situational Awareness AI hedge fund as a possible analogue to Long-Term Capital Management, which blew up roughly two years before the ultimate market top.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: If the analogy holds, a high-profile AI-adjacent blowup is a mid-cycle warning rather than a top signal — historically followed by a melt-up.
insights.quote: Are we going to look back on the unwind of situational awareness similar to the way that we look on long-term capital management?

insights.claim: The hosts argue the real asymmetry in markets is second chances: a retail trader margin-called out of a $5,000 Robinhood account is labeled a degenerate, while the same behavior with billionaire capital is called risk-taking and gets refunded.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A useful lens on why blowups do not deter capital formation at the top of the market — the survivorship is structural, not skill-based.
insights.quote: You probably aren't rich or well-connected enough to have a 24y old incinerate your savings.

themes.theme: Retail speculation, gambling, and prediction market economics

insights.claim: A Bloomberg-cited survey found one quarter of US men aged 18 to 29 say they trade stocks daily and two-thirds of them report feeling like failures, though the hosts think the 25% participation figure is implausibly high.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Quantifies the depth of the young-male retail speculation cohort that drives options and single-stock flow — and its emotional fragility.
insights.quote: One quarter of men aged 18 to 29 said they trade stocks daily.

insights.claim: A Michael Mauboussin and Dan Callahan report cited on the show estimates US gamblers have cumulatively lost $3.9 trillion nominally, or $5.8 trillion in today's dollars, from 1929 to 2025.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of the household wealth transfer to the gambling complex, relevant to sizing the addressable market for prediction market operators.
insights.quote: Gamblers in the US cumulatively lost $3.9 trillion nominally.

insights.claim: The same research shows that on Kalshi the actual win rate versus contract price is almost one-to-one accurate, evidence that prediction markets price odds correctly.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Calibration this tight supports using prediction market prices as a live probability feed for macro and political event risk.
insights.quote: They show the actual win rate versus the contract price on Koshi and it is almost one to one accurate.

insights.claim: A long-shot bias persists in prediction markets: contracts priced near 90 cents win more often than implied because bettors prefer the asymmetric payoff of 10- and 20-cent bets, which is where most losses occur.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: The exploitable edge sits in buying the boring high-probability side that everyone avoids — the same structure as selling lottery-ticket options.

insights.claim: The average vig is cited at about 4.5%, and the host says his own FanDuel account loses roughly seven cents on the dollar, fluctuating between five and nine cents.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A 4-5% starting hole is a hedge-fund-scale fee load, which is why 95%-plus of sports bettors are unprofitable long term.
insights.quote: you're essentially paying like hedge fund fees.

insights.claim: 39% of bettors claim they win more than they lose and 28% claim they break even, against estimates that 95% or more of sports bettors are unprofitable over the long run.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: The gap between perceived and actual results is why gambling and day-trading revenue streams are unusually durable for the operators.
insights.quote: That self assessment contrasts sharply with estimates that 95% or more of sports betterers are unprofitable over the long run.

insights.claim: A Wall Street Journal story describes a 45-year-old accountant who spent almost $1.4 million within four months on the live shopping app WhatNot using savings, personal loans, borrowed money and his employer's credit card, gambling on winning auctions he could resell.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Live-auction commerce is functioning as unregulated gambling, a regulatory tail risk for the category the hosts think should be illegal.
insights.quote: This is some real predatory

themes.theme: Household balance sheets, early retirement, and housing

insights.claim: Bank of America argues the sharp drop in labor force participation for the 55-plus cohort is not workforce discouragement but early retirement driven by higher home values, portfolios and business values.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Reframes a widely-cited bearish labor indicator as a wealth-effect signal, with implications for services demand and structural labor supply.

insights.claim: Bank of America data show the average 401k balance is now about $160,000, up from $100,000 in 2023.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A 60% rise in average retirement balances in two years is the transmission channel from equity gains to consumption and early retirement.
insights.quote: Their average 401k balance is now $160ome thousand. It was $100,000 in 2023.

insights.claim: Conor Sen argues in a new Substack that the housing recession that began in Q1 2022 is over, making it a nearly five-year downturn comparable to 1979-1982, 1988-1991 and 2006-2011.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: A called bottom in housing activity would support homebuilders, mortgage volumes and realtor-linked businesses after a brutal four-year stretch.
insights.quote: The housing recession is over.

insights.claim: The Case-Shiller National Home Price Index is up almost 12% since the first quarter of 2022 despite the housing recession, and prices also rose during the 1979-1982 downturn — meaning most housing recessions are activity recessions, not price declines.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Investors anchored to 2008 as the housing template are mis-modeling downside; the recurring loss is in transaction volume, not home prices.

insights.claim: The hosts describe the housing supply-demand imbalance as permanent, citing roughly 70 million people in their late thirties, boomers not selling, and no plausible path to building enough homes fast enough to matter for young buyers.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Supports structurally higher home prices and rents, and by extension continued affordability-driven political risk in housing policy.

themes.theme: Private-market plumbing, AI narrative management, and media economics

insights.claim: A Wall Street Journal-reported SpaceX SPV chain ran from a Bahamas-based firm called Capital Truth to a New Jersey company called Late Stage, leaving an investor who put in $17,000 in 2020 expecting $300,000 at IPO with $45,000 after the stake was sold in 2024 without his knowledge.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Stacked SPVs on hot pre-IPO names leave end investors unable to verify they hold underlying shares — a due-diligence red flag for all private-access products.
insights.quote: the the investors couldn't even prove that they held underlying shares that they actually had exposure

insights.claim: Mark Zuckerberg has published an essay arguing AI discourse is too dominated by doom and promising everyone a personal agent, a PhD-level tutor and free or affordable access, which the hosts read as a coordinated PR pivot that has come too late.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Signals that AI companies now see public backlash as a business risk — a leading indicator of regulatory and siting friction for data centers.
insights.quote: it is surprising that the discourse for many developing AI is so filled with doom

insights.claim: The hosts question the unit economics of promising free or affordable AI to everyone, asking whether a small paying minority is expected to subsidize the token costs of the mass market.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Frames the core monetization risk in consumer AI: heavy inference costs against a $20/month price point and a large free tier.

insights.claim: Disney reported 7% total revenue growth with 11% growth at parks and experiences that is still accelerating despite continual price increases, alongside the most-watched Q3 for ESPN, ESPN2 and ESPN on ABC since 2016.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Parks pricing power and a sports ratings inflection sit against a stock the hosts call a chronic underperformer relative to its brand strength.

insights.claim: The Toy Story franchise does about $1 billion in annual global retail sales and is estimated to have generated $16 billion in income for Disney.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Quantifies the merchandising annuity behind Disney's IP, the asset that justifies owning the stock despite weak price performance.

insights.claim: Year-to-date box office through August 9th is the highest since before the pandemic, yet IMAX CEO Rich Gelfond gave the hosts the standard answer that new theater construction is too expensive and investors will not fund it.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Supply discipline in premium screens during a record box office year suggests operators view the recovery as non-repeatable — bullish for pricing, bearish for volume growth.
